case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 1014 criminalizes statements that are merely misleading (e.g., true but incomplete) or instead requires proof of a literally false statement.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1014 (prohibiting knowingly making “any false statement or report” for the purpose of influencing certain financial institutions and federal agencies, including the FDIC and FDIC-insured banks).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Thompson argues that § 1014’s text criminalizes only “false” statements—i.e., statements that are untrue—not statements that are merely misleading by omission, implication, or lack of context. He contends both courts below effectively assumed his statements were not literally false yet sustained his conviction by treating misleadingness as sufficient, which conflicts with the ordinary meaning of “false statement,” the rule of lenity, and fair-notice principles. He also emphasizes a circuit split (pointing to cases like Kurlemann) recognizing that § 1014 requires literal falsity, and argues the government’s broader reading invites overcriminalization and dilutes the jury’s role by turning contestable inferences about “misleading” impressions into criminal falsity.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that Thompson in fact made false statements within § 1014’s scope: he affirmatively stated he owed $110,000 when he knew he owed $269,000, and he also misstated the loan’s purpose. On that view, the case does not present (or does not cleanly present) the abstract “misleading but true” question, because the statements at issue were literally incorrect. The government further downplays any asserted circuit conflict, arguing that Seventh Circuit law does not require literal falsity as a categorical matter (or at least has not adopted such a requirement), and that petitioner has not identified controlling Supreme Court or Seventh Circuit authority demanding a literal-falsity-only standard.
key_precedents: United States v. Kurlemann (referenced as an out-of-circuit decision addressing whether § 1014 requires literal falsity)

John Roberts.reasoning: The government’s strongest point—that ordinary usage can label a knowing half-truth “false” in the lending context—still runs headlong into Williams’s rejection of treating implications as “false statements” under § 1014, and expanding “false” to cover contextual misleadingness would broaden a criminal statute without clear notice. Justice Barrett’s observation that Congress routinely says “false or misleading” or targets concealment when it intends to reach half-truths reinforces the structural inference that § 1014 stops at literal falsity. Justice Sotomayor’s Bronston analogy is administrability-confirming: a literal-falsity line is clear and legitimacy-preserving, whereas “misleading impression” invites inference-driven felony liability. Wells does not push us the other way; its refusal to add materiality underscores textual discipline, not an invitation to redefine “false.”

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The government’s strongest point—that ordinary speakers may call a deceptive half-truth “false”—cannot overcome the statutory text in a criminal provision: § 1014 punishes “false statement[s],” which, as Williams indicates, means an objectively untrue factual assertion rather than an “implicit misrepresentation” theory based on context and inferences. Chief Justice Roberts’s fair-notice concern is decisive under a textualist approach: expanding “false” to include truthful-but-misleading answers would effectively add a separate “misleadingness/omission” offense Congress did not enact. Justice Alito and Justice Barrett correctly note Congress routinely uses broader formulations like “false or misleading” or targets concealment when it intends to reach half-truths, and reading “false” to do that work here rewrites the statute. Wells’s text-first method reinforces, rather than undermines, this conclusion, and any residual uncertainty about whether “false” reaches half-truths must be resolved by lenity.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The government’s strongest point is the ordinary-language claim that a deceptive half-truth can be called “false,” especially in bank-lending contexts where the speaker intends to mislead. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Williams draws a workable, notice-protecting line: § 1014 targets objectively untrue factual assertions, not implication-driven “implicit misrepresentation” theories that convert the statute into a general anti-deception provision. Justice Barrett’s structural point is decisive under a textualist approach—Congress knows how to criminalize “false or misleading” statements or concealment, and reading “false” here to include literally true half-truths would effectively amend the statute and expand felony liability without clear notice, triggering lenity. Wells does not push the other way; its refusal to add materiality underscores that we should not add an omission/misleadingness theory either.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The government’s strongest point remains that in ordinary usage a “false statement” can include a half-truth that creates a materially deceptive impression in a lending context, but that reading risks converting § 1014 into a broad anti-deception statute untethered to the text. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Williams is especially persuasive to me: it draws an administrable, fair-notice boundary by requiring an objectively untrue factual assertion rather than an “implicit misrepresentation” theory driven by context and inference. Justice Kagan’s observation that Congress often legislates expressly against “false or misleading” statements (or concealment) reinforces that we should not judicially add an omission/half-truth prohibition to a criminal statute that speaks only of falsity. Given the real-world risk of overcriminalizing imprecise borrower communications—particularly for unsophisticated defendants—lenity properly keeps § 1014 confined to literal falsity, leaving other tools to address sharp but literally true conduct.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The government’s strongest point—flagged by Chief Justice Roberts—that ordinary speakers may call a half-truth “false” in a lending context still runs into the administrable, text-bound line our cases have drawn: § 1014 punishes a “false statement,” and Williams treats that as an objectively untrue factual assertion, not an implication-based theory of deception. Justice Barrett’s structural point is especially persuasive for a textualist: when Congress wants to reach half-truths or omissions it routinely says “false or misleading” or targets “concealment,” and reading “false” here to include truthful-but-misleading speech effectively adds an omission/misleadingness offense Congress did not enact. Justice Sotomayor’s Bronston analogy sharpens the fair-notice problem: a literal-falsity rule provides a clear boundary in criminal law, whereas “false impression” liability invites context-dependent inference and overbreadth. Wells, as multiple colleagues note, reinforces methodological discipline (we don’t add elements), and it gives no warrant to expand “false” beyond literal falsity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The government’s strongest point—that ordinary speakers may call a deceptive half-truth “false,” especially in lending—still asks us to expand a criminal statute from literal falsity to implication-driven misleadingness without textual footing. As the Chief Justice notes, Williams draws a workable line: a “false statement” is an objectively untrue factual assertion, and adopting the respondent’s theory would effectively criminalize omissions and inferences Congress did not name in § 1014. Justice Kagan’s observation that Congress commonly uses formulations like “false or misleading” or separately targets concealment/omissions when it wants broader coverage reinforces the structural inference that “false” alone is narrower here. Even if there is some linguistic tug the other way, the administrability and fair-notice concerns highlighted by Justice Sotomayor (via Bronston) trigger lenity rather than judicial enlargement of felony liability.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The government’s strongest point is that a deceptive half-truth functions like a lie in the lending context, but that functional fraud notion cannot override § 1014’s textual choice of “false statement” rather than “false or misleading” or “conceals.” Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Williams is methodologically persuasive: it draws an administrable, notice-giving line at objectively untrue factual assertions and rejects an “implicit misrepresentation” theory that would turn § 1014 into a broader anti-deception statute. Justice Barrett’s structural point—that Congress knows how to reach misleading half-truths explicitly when it wants to—underscores why expanding “false” here would be an atextual enlargement of criminal liability. Wells reinforces the same discipline: we apply the elements Congress wrote (including falsity as falsity), and any residual ambiguity about half-truths in a felony statute is resolved by fair-notice principles and lenity.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The government’s strongest argument remains that, in ordinary lending discourse, a deceptive half-truth can be called “false” because it predictably conveys a false impression; but in a criminal statute the ordinary public meaning of “false statement” is an actually untrue factual assertion, not a literally true statement that merely invites an inference. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Williams is decisive methodologically: it rejects “implicit misrepresentation” theories under § 1014, and adopting a “misleadingness” test would convert the falsity element into a context-dependent fraud inquiry without the textual markers (e.g., “misleading,” “conceals,” “scheme”) Congress commonly uses. Justice Sotomayor’s Bronston analogue reinforces the administrability and fair-notice line between literal falsity and artfully misleading truth, and any residual uncertainty in this expansionary direction is resolved by lenity. Wells, as Justice Thomas notes, underscores that we enforce § 1014 as written and should not broaden its elements by judicial implication.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The government’s best point is purposive: § 1014 aims to protect banks from deception, and in common parlance a half-truth can be called “false.” But Chief Justice Roberts’s fair-notice and lenity concerns, grounded in Williams’s rejection of “implicit misrepresentation” theories, underscore why we cannot convert that purpose into an atextual “misleadingness” element in a criminal statute. Justice Sotomayor’s Bronston analogy strengthens the administrability and procedural-fairness case: requiring literal falsity avoids context-dependent inferences that risk diluting proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Wells’s text-first methodology, as Justice Kagan notes, cuts against adding materiality there—and likewise counsels against expanding “false” here—so I remain with petitioner.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1014 makes it a crime to “knowingly mak[e] any false statement or report,” and our decision in Williams v. United States treats a “false statement” as a factual assertion capable of being characterized as true or false, not mere deception by implication or omission. Reading “false statement” to include literally true but misleading half-truths would expand a criminal statute beyond its text, raising fair-notice concerns and implicating the rule of lenity, while also risking overbroad federal criminalization in an area Congress could have addressed expressly (e.g., by prohibiting “concealment” or “schemes”). Institutional legitimacy and judicial minimalism counsel adopting the narrower, text-bound rule—§ 1014 requires proof of a statement that is actually false—while leaving to Congress any broader prohibition on misleading omissions. On this record, if the government can prove literal falsity (e.g., misstating the amount owed), the conviction may stand, but the governing legal standard should require falsity, not mere misleadingness.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 1014 criminalizes knowingly making “any false statement or report,” and under its ordinary public meaning “false” denotes a statement that is untrue, not one that is merely misleading by omission or implication. This Court’s decision in United States v. Wells, 519 U.S. 482 (1997), insists on enforcing § 1014’s elements as written—requiring the government to prove a knowingly false statement made with intent to influence—rather than expanding the statute beyond its text. If Thompson’s statements were only arguably misleading but not literally untrue, they fall outside § 1014’s prohibition, and any residual ambiguity must be resolved under the rule of lenity in favor of the accused. The government remains free to prosecute under § 1014 where it proves literal falsity (e.g., an incorrect debt amount), but courts should not dilute “false statement” into a broader “misleading statement” offense without congressional authorization.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1014 makes it a crime to “knowingly mak[e] any false statement or report” to influence covered financial institutions, and the ordinary meaning of “false statement” is a statement that is untrue—not one that is merely misleading by implication or omission. Williams v. United States, 458 U.S. 279 (1982), reflects a restrained, text-bound reading of § 1014 by refusing to expand the statute to cover deceptive conduct (check kiting) absent an actual false “statement,” and that same textual discipline counsels against treating “misleading but literally true” assertions as “false.” Congress elsewhere has shown it knows how to prohibit “false or misleading” statements or omissions that render statements misleading; reading “false” in § 1014 to include mere misleadingness risks surplusage and invites overcriminalization with serious practical consequences for ordinary borrower communications. Whatever the facts of this defendant’s case, the governing legal rule should require proof of literal falsity for § 1014 liability.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1014 criminalizes knowingly making “any false statement or report,” and in a criminal statute that text should be read narrowly to require proof of a statement that is actually untrue, not merely misleading by implication or omission. Extending “false statement” to cover literally true but incomplete answers risks unpredictable, inference-driven prosecutions and undermines fair notice—concerns that the rule of lenity is designed to prevent. Bronston v. United States draws an important line between literal falsity and “literally true but misleading” answers, and while United States v. Wells rejected importing perjury’s elements into § 1014, it still presupposes falsity (and mens rea) rather than a free-floating “misleadingness” standard. If the government can prove Thompson’s statements were in fact incorrect (e.g., misstating the amount owed), it may retry under a literal-falsity theory, but § 1014 should not be stretched to criminalize true-but-misleading statements.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1014 makes it a crime to "knowingly mak[e] any false statement or report" to influence a covered financial institution, and the ordinary meaning of "false statement" connotes a statement that is untrue, not one that is merely misleading by omission. Our § 1014 cases, including United States v. Wells, 519 U.S. 482 (1997), read the statute in a text-focused way and refuse to add elements Congress did not include (there, materiality), which cuts against expanding "false" to cover literally true statements that only create a misleading impression. If Congress wants to criminalize half-truths and omissions, it knows how to do so explicitly (as in other fraud and false-statement regimes), and adopting the government’s broader reading risks workability and fair-notice problems by turning contestable inferences into felony falsity. On this record, to the extent the conviction rests on “misleading but true” theories rather than proof of literal falsity, the rule of lenity and statutory coherence favor petitioner’s narrower construction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1014 makes it a crime to “knowingly mak[e] any false statement or report,” and the ordinary meaning of “false” is untrue, not merely misleading by omission or implication. While United States v. Wells, 519 U.S. 482 (1997), reads § 1014 according to its text and rejects importing extra elements (like materiality), it still presupposes that the government must prove a “false statement”—i.e., a statement that is factually incorrect. If the lower courts sustained the conviction on a theory that concededly true statements can be criminal because they are misleading, that expands the statute beyond its words and raises serious fair-notice concerns; at minimum, ambiguity about whether “false statement” includes truthful-but-misleading half-truths triggers the rule of lenity. The government remains free to retry (or defend) on proof of literal falsity if the record supports it, but § 1014 should not be stretched to cover non-false statements.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1014 makes it a crime to "knowingly ma[k]e any false statement or report" to influence covered financial institutions, and the ordinary meaning of "false statement"—reinforced by fair-notice and lenity principles—requires a statement that is untrue, not merely misleading by implication or omission. Our precedent in United States v. Wells, 519 U.S. 482 (1997), emphasizes fidelity to the statute’s text and rejects importing broader common-law fraud concepts into § 1014; that textual approach counsels against expanding "false" to encompass truthful-but-misleading statements. Practical workability also favors a literal-falsity requirement because it provides a clear, administrable rule for juries and regulated parties, whereas "misleadingness" is context-dependent and risks overcriminalization. The government can still prosecute deceptive conduct when the defendant makes an actually incorrect statement (or under other statutes addressing omissions), but § 1014 should not be stretched beyond its words.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1014’s text makes it a crime to “knowingly mak[e] any false statement or report,” and the ordinary public meaning of “false” is untrue—not merely misleading by omission or implication. Williams v. United States, 458 U.S. 279 (1982), reflects a restrained, text-bound reading of § 1014, rejecting an “implicit misrepresentation” theory and requiring an actual factual assertion capable of being true or false; that reasoning counsels against extending “false statement” to encompass literally true but incomplete statements. Congress elsewhere prohibits “false or misleading” statements or omissions that render statements misleading, reinforcing that “false” in § 1014 should not be read to include “misleading” without surplusage. Because a broader construction would expand criminal liability beyond the statute’s terms and erode fair notice, I would hold § 1014 requires proof of literal falsity.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1014 criminalizes knowingly making “any false statement or report,” and the ordinary meaning of “false” is untrue, not merely misleading by omission or implication. Consistent with Williams v. United States, 458 U.S. 279 (1982), which treated § 1014 as targeting objectively false factual assertions (and not broader banking “misconduct” untethered to falsity), I would read the statute to require proof of literal falsity rather than impressions a jury might deem misleading. That narrower construction promotes procedural fairness and fair notice in criminal law and avoids overcriminalization where Congress could have used broader language (as in other fraud statutes) but did not. If the government believes Thompson’s statements were in fact literally incorrect (e.g., misstating the amount owed), it remains free to prove that falsity on remand under the proper standard.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 1014 criminalizes statements that are merely misleading (e.g., half-truths or omissions) even if they are not literally false.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1014 (prohibiting knowingly making “any false statement or report” for the purpose of influencing certain financial institutions and federal agencies, including the FDIC and insured banks).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Thompson argues that § 1014 reaches only objectively false statements, not statements that are arguably misleading but literally true; he contends the courts below treated his statements as not false yet still upheld liability, which conflicts with the statutory text (“false statement”), ordinary meaning, and fair-notice principles (reinforced by the rule of lenity). He further argues there is a meaningful circuit conflict on whether literal falsity is required under § 1014, and that expanding § 1014 to cover misleadingness effectively turns it into a broader fraud/omission statute without clear congressional authorization, risking vagueness, overcriminalization, and jury-confusion about what the ‘false statement’ element requires.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues Thompson’s conviction fits comfortably within § 1014 because his statements were in fact false—he stated he owed $110,000 when he knew he owed $269,000, and he also misstated the loan’s purpose—so the case does not require the Court to decide whether purely ‘misleading but true’ statements are covered. The government also downplays any circuit split, framing the lower-court decisions as consistent with requiring falsity and treating Thompson’s conduct as involving straightforward falsehoods rather than protected literal truths or mere omissions.
key_precedents: United States v. Kurlemann (cited as an out-of-circuit decision addressing whether § 1014 requires a literally false statement)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Jackson’s procedural point is the most serious: we should not affirm if the jury instructions or the court below allowed conviction on “misleading but literally true” statements, because that would effectively rewrite § 1014’s “false statement” element and raise fair-notice concerns in a criminal case. But I do not read Wells or Williams to require vacatur where the charged statements and verdict rest on affirmative, objectively incorrect factual assertions (as Justice Barrett and Justice Alito emphasize), which fall comfortably within the ordinary meaning of “false” without importing an omissions theory. Consistent with judicial minimalism and institutional restraint, the sound course is to affirm only on that narrow, objective-falsity ground while expressly reserving—and not prejudging—the broader half-truth/omission question flagged by Justices Thomas and Gorsuch. If, on closer inspection of the instructions, the conviction could have rested on literal-truth misleadingness, I would instead favor a limited vacatur/remand, but on the present understanding of the record I would not reverse outright.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s narrow-affirmance proposal—resting on an “objectively false” numerical debt figure—has force if the jury was actually required to find that specific falsity, but it does not answer the central fair-notice problem Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Jackson identify: we cannot affirm by hypothesizing a narrower theory if the instructions or the court below permitted conviction for a merely “misleading” yet literally true statement. Textually, § 1014 punishes a “false statement,” and—as Justice Gorsuch stresses—Congress knows how to criminalize concealment or omissions when it wishes (cf. § 1001), so we should not dilute “false” into “misleading.” Williams and Wells reinforce that we must enforce the statute’s elements as written and avoid enlarging § 1014 beyond objectively untrue factual assertions; if the record is ambiguous on the theory the jury used, lenity and due process require at least vacatur and remand rather than affirmance. Thus, minimalism cannot justify affirming a conviction potentially resting on a legally erroneous, overbroad construction of “false.”

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Jackson’s procedural point is the strongest for Petitioner: we should not affirm a conviction that may have rested on a “misleading but literally true” theory, because § 1014’s text requires a “false statement,” and Williams cautions against stretching that element into broader deceptive conduct. But that concern can be met without reversing the statute’s ordinary meaning where, as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, the charged representation included an affirmative, objectively incorrect numerical debt figure—paradigmatic falsity—so we can affirm while expressly disclaiming any omission/half-truth theory. Justice Thomas’s reliance on § 1001’s concealment language reinforces my view that we must not dilute “false” into “misleading,” yet it does not undermine affirmance on an actually false assertion that falls within § 1014’s core. If there is genuine ambiguity that the instructions or verdict permitted conviction without finding objective falsity, the remedy would be a narrow vacatur/remand on that procedural ground—not a merits holding that narrows § 1014 beyond its plain application to affirmatively false statements.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s minimalist proposal seriously: if the jury necessarily convicted based only on an objectively incorrect numerical debt figure, affirmance could avoid any expansion of § 1014. But Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Jackson’s procedural point is decisive for me—if the Government’s theory or the instructions allowed conviction on “misleading but literally true” statements, we cannot uphold the verdict by relabeling it as “actual falsity” on appeal without undermining fair notice and the statutory element Congress chose. Williams and Wells, as Roberts/Kagan/Barrett invoke them, cut in my direction: they counsel enforcing the word “false” as an objective falsity requirement, not letting courts functionally rewrite § 1014 into an omissions/half-truth statute. Given the real-world consequences in criminal cases, the least we should do is vacate/remand to ensure any conviction rests on a properly cabined falsity theory.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Jackson’s procedural point is the most serious: if the jury was allowed to convict on a “misleading but literally true” theory, affirmance would effectively dilute § 1014’s textual falsity element in a criminal statute, especially given § 1001’s express concealment language and Williams’s insistence on objective falsity. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett that we can—and should—decide narrowly if the charged counts and verdict necessarily rested on affirmative, objectively incorrect factual representations (like misstated debt figures), which are paradigmatically “false statements” without importing an omissions theory. Wells reinforces that restrained approach: we apply the elements as written (including falsity) and need not enlarge § 1014 into a general fraud-by-omission statute. Unless the record shows the instructions/verdict permitted conviction without a finding of objective falsity, I would affirm while expressly reserving the literal-truth/half-truth question.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s narrowest path—affirming on an “objectively false” numerical assertion—directly engages my textual concern and is the strongest Respondent argument. But Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Jackson’s point about the theory presented below remains decisive for me: if the jury instructions or the lower court’s affirmance allowed conviction for something merely misleading yet literally true, we cannot uphold the verdict by appellate relabeling without risking dilution of § 1014’s element of a “false statement.” Wells (as Roberts/Kagan invoke it) reinforces enforcing elements as written; it does not permit redefining “false” to cover half-truths, and Williams counsels against extending § 1014 beyond objectively untrue factual assertions. At minimum, then, the appropriate disposition is vacatur/remand to ensure the conviction rests on actual falsity rather than an omissions/half-truth theory Congress did not enact, consistent with fair notice and lenity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s proposed narrow affirmance on “straightforward, objectively false” numerical assertions is the most substantial Respondent argument, and I agree Wells/Williams require objective falsity rather than an elastic “misleadingness” standard. But as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Jackson stress, if the case was tried or affirmed below on a theory that permitted conviction for literally true but misleading statements, we cannot affirm by recasting the basis for the verdict on appeal without creating fair-notice and legitimacy problems in a criminal case. The § 1001 comparison (Thomas/Gorsuch) reinforces that Congress knows how to criminalize concealment and omissions, and we should not silently import that into § 1014. Institutionally, the cleaner course is vacatur/remand to ensure the conviction (if it stands) rests solely on an objective-falsity theory the jury was actually required to find, while expressly reserving the broader half-truth question.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point: § 1014’s text speaks of a “false statement,” and ordinary meaning (reinforced by Williams and Congress’s separate concealment language in § 1001) does not naturally extend to literally true half-truths or omissions, so we should not affirm on a “misleadingness” construction. I agree with that textual limit, but I remain persuaded by the Chief Justice’s narrower approach that the verdict can be sustained on affirmative, objectively untrue factual representations (e.g., incorrect numerical debt figures), which fit “false” without expanding the statute. Justice Kavanaugh’s procedural concern is serious; if the instructions or theory below permitted conviction absent objective falsity, the proper remedy would be vacatur and remand rather than affirmance. On my current understanding of the record, we can affirm while expressly reserving—and disclaiming—any holding that § 1014 reaches literal truths, omissions, or half-truths.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s narrow affirmance—treating the conviction as resting on an objectively false numerical debt figure—has force, but it does not answer the procedural-fairness problem Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Gorsuch identify: if the jury instructions or the Government’s theory permitted conviction on “misleading but literally true” statements, we cannot affirm by recasting the case on appeal. Williams and the § 1001 concealment contrast, emphasized by Justice Thomas, underscore that § 1014’s text requires objective falsity, and Wells’s element-focused approach cuts against diluting that requirement into a broader misleadingness standard. As a pragmatic matter, vacatur/remand is the least disruptive remedy that protects fair notice and ensures any conviction rests on the statute Congress wrote rather than an elastic omissions theory. Unless the record clearly shows the jury necessarily found objective falsity as the basis for guilt, I would not affirm.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1014 criminalizes “knowingly mak[ing] any false statement or report” to influence an insured bank or covered federal agency, and the Government’s account describes straightforward literal falsity (e.g., misstating the amount owed) that falls within the statute’s text. Given the case can be resolved on the narrow ground that Thompson’s representations were actually false, I would avoid deciding the broader question whether § 1014 reaches half-truths or omissions that are merely misleading, preserving institutional legitimacy and adhering to minimalism. Our precedent in United States v. Wells underscores an appropriately text-bound approach to § 1014 and counsels against adding or subtracting elements beyond what Congress specified, which here is satisfied if the statement is false. On this record, affirmance does not require endorsing an expansive “misleading-but-true” theory, and we should not reach it.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 1014 criminalizes knowingly making “any false statement or report,” and the ordinary public meaning of “false” at enactment does not naturally encompass statements that are merely misleading, literally true half-truths, or omissions. As in Williams v. United States, 458 U.S. 279 (1982), this Court should not expand § 1014 beyond its terms to reach conduct Congress did not clearly criminalize; if Congress wishes to prohibit misleading-but-true statements, it must say so. Extending § 1014 to cover “misleadingness” risks vagueness and undermines fair notice, and any residual ambiguity in a criminal statute must be resolved in favor of the accused under the rule of lenity. Accordingly, § 1014 should be read to require an objectively false statement, and convictions premised on non-false “misleading” statements cannot stand.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1014 criminalizes knowingly making “any false statement or report,” and on this record Thompson’s statements were not merely misleading half-truths but affirmatively false factual assertions (e.g., representing he owed $110,000 when he knew he owed $269,000), bringing the case comfortably within the statute’s text. Williams v. United States, 458 U.S. 279 (1982), underscores a narrow, text-focused reading of § 1014 by declining to extend it to conduct (check kiting) that was not a “factual assertion” capable of being true or false; here, by contrast, Thompson made factual assertions. Because the conviction can be sustained on straightforward falsity, the Court need not decide whether § 1014 reaches omissions or literally true but misleading statements, and there is no occasion to expand the statute or invoke lenity. Practical consequences also counsel against upsetting a conviction involving clear falsehoods in bank-lending applications that Congress plainly sought to deter through § 1014.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1014’s text criminalizes only a knowingly made “false statement or report,” and in a criminal statute that language should be read to require objective falsity, not merely a misleading half-truth or omission. Extending § 1014 to literally true but arguably deceptive statements risks unfair notice, jury confusion about what the “false statement” element requires, and overcriminalization—concerns that counsel a narrower reading under fair-warning principles and the rule of lenity. While United States v. Wells, 519 U.S. 482 (1997), emphasized § 1014’s specific elements (knowledge of falsity and intent to influence) and rejected importing extra elements like materiality, that textual approach likewise supports confining liability to statements that are actually false rather than merely misleading. If Congress wants to reach omissions or broader deceptive conduct, it can do so explicitly, as in other fraud provisions, rather than by stretching “false statement” beyond its ordinary meaning.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1014’s text criminalizes knowingly making “any false statement or report” to influence an insured bank, and the statute’s scienter and purpose requirements already meaningfully cabin liability. On this record, Thompson’s statements are best understood as straightforward falsehoods (e.g., stating he owed $110,000 while knowing he owed substantially more), so the Court need not decide the harder question whether purely “misleading but literally true” half-truths fall within § 1014. Consistent with United States v. Wells, § 1014 is not a freewheeling fraud statute, but it does reach knowing falsity intended to influence a covered institution, and that workably resolves this case without expanding the statute to pure omissions. Any broader debate about “literal truth” akin to Bronston arises in a distinct perjury context and does not control the interpretation of § 1014’s “false statement” language.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1014 criminalizes knowingly making “any false statement or report,” and the ordinary meaning of “false” requires an objectively untrue assertion—not a merely misleading half-truth or omission. In Williams v. United States, 458 U.S. 279 (1982), the Court construed § 1014 narrowly, refusing to treat conduct as a “false statement” when it did not constitute a factual misrepresentation in the relevant sense, reinforcing that courts may not expand the statute beyond its text. Where Congress wishes to reach concealment or misleading omissions, it knows how to say so (as in 18 U.S.C. § 1001(a)(1)’s “conceals or covers up”), and reading that concept into § 1014 would raise fair-notice concerns and invite overcriminalization—triggering the rule of lenity in any genuine ambiguity. Because the question presented asks whether “misleading but literally true” statements suffice, I would hold they do not under § 1014’s plain terms.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1014 criminalizes “any false statement or report,” and the ordinary meaning of “false” requires an objectively untrue assertion, not a merely misleading half-truth or omission. As in Williams v. United States, 458 U.S. 279 (1982), we should resist expanding § 1014 beyond its text to reach conduct Congress did not clearly cover—there, the Court refused to treat check-kiting as a “false statement” because a check is not a factual assertion, reflecting a tradition of narrow construction of federal criminal statutes. Reading “false statement” to include literal truths that are only misleading would create serious fair-notice and workability problems, effectively converting § 1014 into a broader fraud/omission statute without clear authorization, and the rule of lenity counsels against that expansion. The government may still prevail on remand if it proves Thompson’s statements were actually false, but the lower courts should not affirm liability on a “misleading but true” theory under § 1014.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1014’s text criminalizes knowingly making “any false statement or report” to influence covered financial institutions, and on this record Thompson’s statements appear to be straightforward factual falsehoods (e.g., misstating his debt amount), so the conviction can be sustained without expanding the statute to cover merely misleading but literally true half-truths or omissions. Williams v. United States, 458 U.S. 279 (1982), underscores a textual limit: conduct that is deceptive but not a “factual assertion” cannot be deemed “true” or “false” under § 1014, which supports deciding this case on falsity rather than adopting a broader misleadingness theory. Preserving that limiting principle respects fair notice and methodological consistency while leaving for another day whether § 1014 reaches literally true but misleading statements. Given the government’s characterization that the statements were in fact false, I would affirm on that narrower ground consistent with the statute’s ordinary meaning and precedent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1014 criminalizes knowingly making “any false statement or report,” and that text—especially in a criminal statute—demands an objectively false assertion, not mere misleadingness through half-truths or omissions. Williams v. United States, 458 U.S. 279 (1982), reflects the Court’s reluctance to expand § 1014 beyond its terms where Congress has not clearly covered broader deceptive conduct, reinforcing fair-notice and anti-overcriminalization concerns. Treating literally true but misleading statements as “false statements” risks vagueness and invites convictions based on imprecise standards, contrary to procedural fairness and the rule of lenity. On this record, if Thompson’s answers are not actually false as charged, § 1014 should not be stretched to function as an omissions or fraud statute without clearer congressional direction.
